chapters.title: Basic principles of the event
chapters.description: What applies, fair play, the organiser's word.
chapters.body_html:
Pán Prstenů is a LARP battle set in the world of J. R. R. Tolkien (the era of the "War of the Ring"). The event is a game, not a simulation of real combat. The purpose of the game is fun and a pleasant way of spending free time.

  • Thematic setting: set in the world of J. R. R. Tolkien.
  • Realism: unrealistic and out-of-setting equipment will not be allowed.
  • Ignorance of the rules is no excuse.
  • You came here to have fun, not to argue.
  • Be considerate of nature and the people around you.
  • Play fair. Anyone who does not know what that means stays at home.
  • The organiser has the final word. Do not argue with them.
  • Players are obliged to read the rules and follow them. Failure to comply with them or with the organisers' instructions may lead to your removal from the battle.
  • The laws of the Czech Republic apply, and ignorance of them is also no excuse.
  • No means no!
  • The organiser may, before or during the event, ban any weapon and even confiscate it for the rest of the game if they see fit.
  • Please observe the rules of decent camping (see Participation and behaviour in camp).
  • Fires may only be lit in places designated and prepared by the organiser.
  • No smoking in the forest. Smoking during the game is therefore forbidden.
  • Players are obliged to look after, above all, THEIR OWN combat qualities, THEIR OWN acknowledgement of hits, THEIR OWN costume standard, etc. Want to complain about another player? Each army has its main NPC organiser — turn to them and the matter will be dealt with.
  • You may take part in the battle only in a state that does not raise doubts about your physical and mental fitness. Objective grounds may be ongoing intoxication by alcohol or other substances, but also the organiser's subjective judgement (e.g. a strong hangover, illness, uncontrollable bursts of aggression).
  • Participants under the influence of alcohol will not be admitted to any part of the event.
  • If a dispute arises during the battle, the organiser's decision always applies. If no organiser is present, turn to the nearest available ruler to settle the dispute provisionally.
  • Safety comes first!

In-game — quick overview

  • The minimum number of lives is 2, the maximum is 4 (see Costume rating). Lives are assigned on Saturday morning before the battle during the costume check.
  • Every weapon strike counts as 1 life.
  • An archer's arrow counts as 2 lives.
  • Hit zones are the so-called "large" ones: torso, legs from the torso to the ankles and arms from the torso to the wrists (see Hit zones and lives).
  • The hit is acknowledged by the person who was hit.
  • Death is played out. If you can, lie down. Resurrection takes place at the standard (see Death and resurrection).
  • Weapons must be safe, of realistic dimensions and craftsmanship, made of suitable material and aesthetic — they are part of the costume (see Weapons).
  • All arrows must have approved safe heads, a nock on the shaft and fletchings.

chapters.title: Participation and behaviour in camp
chapters.body_html:
Behaviour, safety and respect

  • Whatever the organiser says goes!
  • If any organiser forbids something (lighting a fireplace, fails to approve a weapon), only that organiser or the head organiser may later allow it. Attempts to circumvent this rule will be rewarded by the irrevocability of the ban.
  • The legal order of the Czech Republic applies at the event. We expressly advise against breaking the rules of misdemeanour and criminal law (do not steal others' arrows, do not harm anyone's health, do not serve alcohol to minors) and the laws on the protection of nature (fire in the forest, gathering wood, water protection).
  • At the event, respect everyone's personal boundaries and treat each other with respect. Any physical contact should be based on the consent of both/all parties involved. No simply means no. If you need to talk to someone, a confidential support person (male and female) will be present at the event.
  • The event takes place in a location subject to nature protection law. Serious or repeated breaches of the rules are grounds for exclusion from the event without compensation (refund of the registration fee).
  • Each participant needs their own costume, weapon and water bottle for the battle. Bring more weapons rather than fewer, in case one is not approved during the check. Camping is in your own tents.

Camping, fire, waste and substances

  • A costume requirement applies throughout the entire event. Strolling about "in civvies" will be taken as an offer to be drafted into the organiser's work crew. If you are accompanying your child, sew yourself at least a cloak/robe in a non-disruptive colour at home.
  • From 22:00 on Friday onwards, quiet hours apply in the camp and surrounding area. We all need to be fit on Saturday.
  • Fires may only be lit in the camp, and only in fireplaces approved and prepared by the organisers. Setting up your own fireplaces is permitted only with the explicit consent of an organiser. Within the camp, the use of portable braziers and grills that do not damage the lawn and do not let embers fall to the ground is allowed.
  • Setting up fireplaces or otherwise significantly interfering with nature and the landscape at the event location is permitted only with the explicit consent of an organiser.
  • Throw rubbish into the bin bags supplied in advance.
  • Smoking is strictly forbidden throughout the entire game area. In camp, e.g. by the fires, you may smoke if it does not bother anyone present.
  • Anyone under the influence of alcohol or other intoxicating substances will not be admitted to the battle. We do not rule out spot checks before the battle. During the battle, any consumption of such substances is strictly forbidden.
  • After the event, only flattened grass should remain in the meadow. No holes left by stakes, no buried fireplaces, no scattered rubbish.

What will be provided at the event

  • Portable toilets (toi-toi type).
  • Drinking water from a delivered tank.
  • A tavern with three meals a day. We recommend bringing your own tankard and bowl — plastic ones will incur a fee.
  • Firewood from supplies brought by the organisers or by gathering fallen wood. No felling of trees.
  • What will not be provided: mobile signal, power sockets, a water source for bathing.

chapters.title: Combat — hits and techniques
chapters.body_html:
Basic rules of a hit

  • Every strike must be delivered with a visible swing. No flailing!
  • Every strike must be pulled; blows must not land at full force.
  • The hafts of axes, hammers and polearms do not cause a hit.
  • An arrow hit only counts when made by the head and only if the arrow does not continue in flight.
  • The validity of a hit is decided by the person who was hit.
  • You are obliged, immediately after a hit or whenever asked, to truthfully state your remaining lives. E.g.: "I have three.", "Two more.", "Zero, I'm dead."
  • Hits delivered simultaneously by several opponents add up.
  • In a simultaneous hit (mutual hit within about 1 second), both opponents are wounded.
  • The permitted combat technique is thrusting with spears and slashing with other contact weapons.
  • Both slash and thrust must be delivered with a visible arm swing (definitely not by wrist motion only). Two-handed weapons must be wielded with both hands. Weapons and projectiles must stop at their target and not continue in flight, slash or other movement. Any movement of the weapon must be controlled at all times, and hitting the opponent must be done with intensity corresponding to the appearance of the person hit (a fifteen-year-old beanpole in a tunic vs. a hundred-kilo Viking in mail).
  • An overly "gentle" hit, if it otherwise meets the above (i.e. the opponent could have hit you but chose not to), is not grounds to disregard the hit, provided you visually registered it.

In combat you MAY NOT

  • Use any form of physical attack, punches, kicks, blows with the weapon's pommel, leg sweeps, throwing down, grabbing and holding the opponent, locks, wrestling, blocking another's blade with your own body (and the subsequent swatting with a short weapon) — basically anything where the bodies of the fighters come into mutual contact.
  • Abuse physical superiority to gain an advantage in combat. E.g. it is allowed to attack the opponent's shield with a spear so they have to keep holding it in the direction of the attack — but it is not allowed to attack the shield with such force as to push it and its owner a metre back.
  • Grab a weapon by the blade or edge, or grab the opponent's shield.
  • Push your opponent into dangerous terrain during combat.
  • Attack or push someone with a shield (especially from a charge).

In combat you MAY

  • Catch the attacker's forearm at the hand holding the weapon, the sword's hilt, the haft or shaft of the weapon. The permitted holding time is 3 seconds.

Safety

  • In case of any painful hit (especially to the head), the person hit has the right to interrupt the fight for as long as needed — placing a hand on the head means "I'm out of the game".
  • If you injure an opponent, you must immediately provide the necessary help and call a medic.
  • In dangerous places, all kinds of fighting are prohibited.
  • All players are obliged to watch the terrain in which the fight takes place and not to push opponents into dangerous terrain (e.g. piles of fallen branches). They must warn a retreating opponent and look out for their safety as well.
  • If you feel that someone is fighting unfairly, assume they are doing so out of ignorance and politely point it out. If it turns out they are an idiot, it is best to stop playing with them and move to another part of the battlefield.

chapters.title: Hit zones and lives
chapters.body_html:
Combat is fought to the so-called large hit zones. Hits here count. Outside them hits do not count, and deliberately attacking these areas is against the rules.

Hits here COUNT

  • torso
  • arms from the torso to the wrists
  • legs from the torso to the ankles

Hits here DO NOT COUNT

  • head
  • neck
  • groin
  • arms from the wrists down (inclusive)
  • legs from the ankles down (inclusive)
  • If a hit lands on both a valid and an invalid hit zone, it does not count.
  • All valid hit zones are equal — a hit on an arm or leg has the same value as a hit to the chest, belly or back.
  • It is forbidden to use invalid hit zones as cover. This rule also applies to a fighting stance that hides valid hit zones behind invalid ones (typically a forward-leaning stance with an unprotected head sticking out in front of the body).

Loss of lives

  • A melee weapon hit to a valid hit zone removes 1 life.
  • A ranged weapon hit (bow, crossbow) to a valid hit zone removes 2 lives.
  • When you lose your last life (state of 0 lives), you are mortally wounded (see Death and resurrection).
  • The number of lives you bring into the battle depends on the costume rating (see Costume rating) — 2 to 4 lives.

chapters.title: Death and resurrection
chapters.description: What to do after death, resurrection at the standard.
chapters.body_html:
When you lose your last life

  • At 0 lives you are mortally wounded.
  • If you have resurrections available in the given game phase (you will be told before each engagement), you fall (step aside, crawl) out of the engagement and, with one hand behind your head, silently and without further interfering with the engagement, move to your resurrection spot — your army banner (standard).
  • If you have no resurrections in the given game phase, you remain mortally wounded lying where the enemy overcame you.

A mortal wound is played out

The mortally wounded collapses on the spot, where they lie quiet and motionless. From time to time someone may groan with pain, rasp and otherwise atmospherically contribute to the impression of a battlefield strewn with the dying.

Don't overdo it! The dead do not stand around or have out-of-game conversations. Do not ruin the atmosphere. As a mortally wounded character you do not interfere with the game in any other way (including talking).

If you risk being trampled at the place of the engagement, you may stagger off and fall a short distance further, or, while already lying down, crawl a bit to the side.

chapters.title: Weapons — permitted, dimensions, combinations
chapters.body_html:
All weapons used at the event must be approved by an organiser. Anyone caught fighting with an unapproved weapon faces: the certain confiscation of the weapon for the rest of the event; the possibility that the weapon will be destroyed; and the possibility of being asked to leave the event.

Permitted weapons Dimensions Notes
Short weapons (one-handed) up to 90 cm —
Flail up to 75 cm Haft 40 cm, chain + fully soft ball 35 cm. The chain must be solid (e.g. an unfrayed rope or a yekor chain).
Long weapons (hand-and-a-half, two-handed) up to 120 cm Cannot be combined with anything.
Spear up to 200 cm Combinations with a shield are allowed; spear up to 150 cm at most.
Shields up to 250 cm in perimeter Organisers will look critically at shields of dubious shapes that try to use up the permitted dimensions to the maximum (so-called "barn doors").
For shields with any dimension exceeding 60 cm, functional head protection (gambeson + mail coif, a solid leather/iron helmet) is mandatory equipment for the fighter.
Bows / crossbows 15 kg / 150 N With a minimum ammunition of 10 arrows/bolts (see Bows, crossbows and arrows).
Permitted combinations total weapon length up to 150 cm One-hander + cleaver, one-hander + dagger, cleaver + cleaver.

Thematic setting

  • The game is set in the world of J. R. R. Tolkien's books, the era of the "War of the Ring". Your weapons and costumes should respect the event's setting.
  • We use weapons that "copy" or imitate medieval European and Middle-Eastern weapons.
  • Weapons outside the event's time setting will not be permitted — firearms (pistols, blunderbusses), small swords, rapiers, etc.

Realism

The weapon you will use at the event should have realistic dimensions and look like a weapon. For inspiration we recommend the book by Eduard Wagner — Cutting and Thrusting Weapons (taking into account the period being represented).

A weapon must look like a weapon and is part of the costume!

An aesthetically unsuitable appearance is grounds for not approving a weapon. We will certainly not approve: bladed weapons without crossguards or basket hilts, foam clubs or mirelon cylinders and weapons in unsuitable, garish colours (see also Weapons — safety and aesthetics).

chapters.title: Weapons — safety and aesthetics
chapters.body_html:
Safety

  • All weapons must be padded with at least 1.5 cm of mirelon foam, ideally combined with yekor and a sleeping mat. The padding must be functional (cushioning the impact) and not worn out. Along edges and rounded sides the weapon must be carefully and sufficiently softened.
  • The upper third of the hafts of axes, hammers, maces and similar weapons must also be padded. Axe blades must flex resiliently on impact — but not at the cost of the hit area striking the haft.
  • The padding must not give way on impact in such a way that there is a risk of being hit by an unpadded part of the weapon.
  • Shield edges must not be chipped or splintered and must be softly rounded. Straight, unrounded shield edges, no matter how well wrapped, will 99% mean your shield is not approved for the game. Wrapping the rounded edge in leather or thin garden hose (hidden under leather, or, at worst, carpet tape) is enough as softening. The shield's surface must be rounded with no sharp edges or protrusions (especially important on bosses and places with metal joints).
  • Weapons and other equipment must have no sharp edge, even underneath the padding. The weapon or shield must not have any loose part or any (not just metal) protrusions.
  • Weapons must not contain any loose or detached parts.
  • The owner must demonstrate the ability to handle the weapon safely.
  • Weapons that are too light (bamboo and similar light materials) or uncontrollably heavy do not belong in the game and will not be admitted. This applies in particular, but not exclusively, to hammers, maces and axes. The weight of a weapon will be assessed with regard to the owner's ability to control it.

Basic equipment requirements

  • A weapon is part of your character's costume. You can have the most beautiful scale armour, but a round, oblong object without a crossguard and with the red carpet tape peeling off will drag your whole effort down by quite a few floors.
  • Safety — A weapon that fails the weapon check may be confiscated for the rest of the game, in which case you will have nothing to fight with.
  • Realistic dimensions — No mega-clubs or super-axes. No "swords" like a paddle (blades over 10 cm wide). Avoid unnecessarily massive padding on shield edges ("the mirelon flounce").
  • Realistic execution — A sword has a crossguard and a flat blade (it is not round). An axe has a shaped edge. A hammer is not a shapeless block of foam. A spear is not a dildo or a knob on a stick (but it must still be safe). A shield is round, heater-shaped or kite-shaped — no barn doors, no hexagons or polygons with more sides.
  • Suitable material — Skip shiny and visibly modern materials. Carpet (yekor), leatherette and fake fur are unsuitable as a shield cover. Do not use carpet tape in unsuitable colours (red, green, blue). On the other hand, brown, grey and black are fine. Grey power tape on a blade is acceptable. No insulating tape! A black smooth surface of weapons coated in Balakryl is acceptable. The ideal is dyed weapons with a metal patina.
  • Aesthetics — A weapon must look at least somewhat decent. No bits of peeling carpet tape and dried mud. Beauty lies in simplicity.
The organisers reserve the right not to admit, or to remove during the event, any weapon or piece of equipment which, in their opinion, is damaged, unsafe, not in keeping with the event's theme, ugly or otherwise unsuitable. At their discretion they may confiscate such a weapon until the end of the event.

chapters.title: Forbidden weapons
chapters.body_html:
There is a small group of weapons or combinations thereof that we do not allow at the event:

  • All unpadded or poorly padded weapons.
  • All oversized weapons. For safety reasons — our event accommodates younger players and newcomers, and fighting with such weapons requires a certain level of experience.
  • No fighting staves, scythes or other slashing or crushing polearms such as long halberds, glaives, flails, etc. This category also includes war scythes.
  • All variations of Far-Eastern weapons. Typically samurai swords.
  • Weapons from other fantasy worlds and games which break the theme even if nicely made (no Warhammer, Warcraft, anime or similar nonsensical contraptions and inventions).

chapters.title: Bows, crossbows and arrows
chapters.body_html:
Bows and crossbows

  • Bows or crossbows are usually shop-bought. No modern sport or compound bows. A "children's bow", i.e. a fibreglass stick with a PVC grip, is also entirely unsuitable.
  • The bowstring should not be a shiny synthetic cord.
  • Don't forget the quiver.
  • We will not aesthetically rate the arrows — for arrows we focus on safety. But if an arrow is also nicely styled (feather fletchings, head in a non-disruptive colour, stained shaft), all the better.
  • Both bow and crossbow must have a draw weight of at most 15 kg / 150 N.
  • The arrow must be softened by a ball or a cylinder with a diameter perpendicular to the shaft of at least 5 cm, with the front part fitted with foam at least 3 cm deep (head).
  • The shaft of the arrow must be properly secured against being driven through the head, and the head must hold firmly on the shaft so that it cannot under any circumstances slip off.
  • The organisers have the right to randomly verify the manufacturing technology of every type of arrow submitted, even at the cost of destroying it.
  • All arrows must be approved individually by an organiser.
  • The minimum is 10 approved arrows / bolts per shooter. If at least ten arrows are not approved for someone, their bow will not be approved either.

Rules for arrows (heads, shaft, fletchings)

  • The head must be attached so that it does not loosen or slip off by itself with repeated use of the arrow.
  • The shaft must have a solid base that prevents it from being driven through the head (e.g. a PET bottle cap or a fresh cork). This solid core must be wrapped from the side and from the front to form a soft head with a diameter of at least 5 cm.
  • The head must not contain any sharp or metal object.
  • An arrow with an unsuitable head will not be approved.
  • The shaft of a wooden arrow should have a diameter of min. 8 mm (smaller diameters break easily). For a fibreglass shaft, a smaller diameter is possible.
  • Each arrow must be fitted with a nock (groove) for placing it on the bowstring.
  • Each arrow must be fitted with fletchings made of suitable material — feathers or a synthetic equivalent, "power tape" tape, material without sharp edges. Arrows without fletchings will not be approved (an arrow without fletchings tends to flip in flight, shaft first).
  • Flu-flu (frayed fletching around the shaft) or a stabilising "bundle" of strings can also be used.

Collecting arrows and fair play

  • Archers are obliged after the game ends to gather all foreign arrows at a place designated by the organisers and exchange them with others for their own. If you cannot find the owner, leave foreign arrows with the organisers.
  • An archer has under no circumstances the right to take an arrow that does not belong to them. That is theft.
  • You may only shoot with your own ammunition or with that of fellow fighters with whom you have an arrangement. Place foreign arrows in piles along the paths, where their owners will collect them.
  • It is forbidden to fight with a damaged weapon or shield until it is repaired and re-approved by an organiser.
The organisers warn that using unapproved and dangerous arrows at the event may be classified as a criminal offence with all its consequences (especially the use of arrows with a head incapable of preventing injury by the shaft).

chapters.title: Costume rating (2–4 lives)
chapters.body_html:
Players are assigned 2 to 4 lives. The main criterion is the overall impression of the costume — how well the player succeeds in capturing the attire of a member of a given nation. Any armour will not add lives if it does not fit the costume. On the other hand, you can get the full number of lives without wearing a single piece of iron.

Categories by number of lives

0 lives

If you turn up in a perfectly elaborated Pikachu or pink pony costume, we'll send you to change or send you home.

1 life

In rare cases of a young beginner in a tragic "costume" we will at least reward them with participation in the game. If you are reading this, hopefully it will not be your case.

2 lives — basic soldier

A simple tunic and trousers/breeches, complemented by at least an improvised belt with some personal item (a pouch, a beggar's bag, etc.). Reasonably disguised civilian shoes. For elves of course ears, for dwarves a beard, for orcs make-up, for Haradrim a turban or scarf. Hands protected by gloves.

Example: an orc with a blackened face, a torn tunic and trousers, simple black gloves, no headgear, simple weapons, on the feet non-disruptive modern shoes wrapped in cloth.

3 lives — elaborate costume

A basic soldier supplemented by decorative elements of clothing (embroidered or fur trim, jewellery, amulets) and additional layers of the costume — surcoats, tunics, gambesons. Footwear better matches the clothing (period-style shoes, opanci and leg wraps). An effort to protect life with at least some armour (a gambeson, vambraces, a shorter mail shirt, shin guards) and visible head protection (a reinforced collar, a sturdier cap, an arming cap, a helmet). At three lives we also expect the weapons to be in order — aesthetically matching the army.

Example: a dwarf soldier in baggy trousers, a long tunic to the knees (visually shortening the figure), a quilted gambeson, a surcoat with a contrasting border, reinforced gloves, a padded cap, opanci with leg wraps.

4 lives — a veteran at first sight

The costume is more like clothing, functional for life in the field. All parts of the clothing have elaborate detail, are mutually coordinated and functionally connected. The wearer's way of life and their social class are evident from the costume. Clothing, accessories and weapons are individualised — specifically shaped, complemented by coats of arms, personal marks, embossing of leather elements or other decoration. Front-line men protect themselves with solid gambesons, mail armour and individual pieces of plate armour. Their heads are covered by hoods or helmets of metal or thick leather. Archers or light infantry are armoured less, but more practically.

Balancing costume elements

The aim is to meet as many of the defining features of the given category as possible. If something pulls your costume into a lower category, balance it with something that pulls you up again (e.g. you don't have solid headgear, but you have nice shoes, mail armour and a tricked-out robe). Stick to common sense — the costume must form a harmonious whole (don't pair an ornately decorated helmet with a plume with the simple costume of a basic soldier).

Full plate armour and heavy armour

We don't really recommend it. The setting of the event assumes a clash of ordinary, second-rate units; heroes and veterans in full plate armour are, by the story's logic, elsewhere on the map. The atmosphere of Middle-earth is much better evoked by quality costumes described above under numbers 4 and 3 than by an (admittedly impressive) heap of iron.

In addition, even if the organiser awards you the maximum number of lives, there will be equally lifed players on the battlefield wearing significantly fewer kilograms. If we still don't put you off, do not forget to complement the armour with suitable non-iron parts of the costume that clearly place you with one of the in-game nations.

What is almost certainly wrong

  • Costumes that don't fit the world of The Lord of the Rings (Warcraft, Na'vi, etc.).
  • Re-enactor clothing not respecting the stylistic and colour palette of the armies (too much red, Landsknecht clothing).
  • Ignoring national specifics (un-blackened orcs, Haradrim without a "towel", beardless dwarves).
  • Palestinian scarves on Haradrim.
  • For girls, variants of "bra" armour, exposed cleavage, bare midriffs — these don't belong in the battle.
  • Pirates of the Caribbean for Umbar.
  • Necromancer/undead combinations (although in a well-conceived Umbar–Dark Númenor it can have a place as a partial motif).
  • Atmospheric characters not arranged with the organisers (Aragorn, Legolas, Gandalf, Nazgûl, etc.).

Details of the individual armies are in the Armies and sides section. Tips for making a costume are in the Guides for newcomers section.

chapters.title: Guides for newcomers
chapters.description: What you need to know the first time.
chapters.body_html:
You don't have anything to wear to the battle and want to make your gear yourself, but you don't know how? Don't despair. The Czech LARP battle scene has produced so many good guides that there really is plenty to choose from.

Recommended articles on larp.cz

A good start is the articles published by Orzo on larp.cz. In particular, "Before, at and after your first LARP" for complete newcomers:

  • Before, at and after your first LARP
  • How to make a costume, getting started
  • Even a LARP costume should make sense: part 1 — Order of acquisition
  • Even a LARP costume should make sense: part 2 — Inspiration from history
  • Character personality and costume

Communities and other resources

  • The FB group LARP CZ and LARP forums — guides, inspiration, advice straight from others.
  • BOT — orc world — a forum bringing together orcs, goblins and similar creatures. You will find there many quality guides on orc clothing, armour, masks, etc.
Tip for newcomers: don't overdo it on your first event. A simple but thematically fitting costume for 2 lives is a better choice than half a year of stress over full plate armour.

footer_alert.title: Full text of the rules and updates
footer_alert.body_html: The full text of the rules for this year's event (PDF) will be published by 15 July 2026 and sent to all registered participants. If you find an inconsistency in the text or have a question, contact us at info@panprstenu.cz.
